flashcard_questions.q: Who was the anatomist Andreas Vesalius?
flashcard_questions.a: A Flemish anatomist who carried out his own human dissections.

flashcard_questions.q: How many mistakes did Vesalius prove Galen had made?
Why had Galen’s anatomy been wrong?
flashcard_questions.a: He had only dissected animals such as monkeys and pigs.

flashcard_questions.q: Which bone did Vesalius show was a single bone, not two?
In which year did Vesalius publish On the Fabric of the Human Body?
What spread Vesalius’s corrected anatomy across Europe?
What did Galen wrongly claim happened to blood?
flashcard_questions.a: It was made in the liver and burned up by the body.

flashcard_questions.q: What did William Harvey prove about the heart?
flashcard_questions.a: That it acts as a pump, pushing blood through arteries and veins.

flashcard_questions.q: In which year did Harvey publish his work on circulation?
Why did Harvey’s discovery have little practical use at the time?
flashcard_questions.a: Blood transfusions were not yet possible.

flashcard_questions.q: Which vessels could Harvey not see with the microscopes of his day?
What was the standard treatment for gunshot wounds before Paré?
flashcard_questions.a: Burning the wound with boiling oil, called cauterisation.

flashcard_questions.q: Which ingredient did Paré add to egg yolk and rose oil?
What did Paré use ligatures for?
flashcard_questions.a: Tying off arteries with silk threads after amputation.

flashcard_questions.q: What did Paré’s Bezoar Stone experiment prove?
flashcard_questions.a: The stone had no power to cure poison.

notes: 15 cards: 5 person-to-significance, 4 term/technique, 3 event/date, 3 cause-effect. Split the Hippocrates-style stuffed cards into one fact each; Vesalius, Harvey and Paré each get their own block.
